items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] MoMA explores the useful beauty of information design
items.content_html:
When people post infographics on their Instagram accounts, they’re sharing information and facts about the world with their followers. They’re also trying to convey something about the kind of person they are by distributing these aesthetically pleasing, digestible bites of data. Perhaps they want to make a statement about their own politics or conscientiousness. 

So what is the Museum of Modern Art revealing about itself as an institution with its forthcoming exhibit Full Disclosure: The Edge of Information Design?

The pieces of information design in the exhibition “tell us the fact that the museum is always ready to understand what’s important to the world in that particular moment, and to try to give the best examples of it,” says Paola Antonelli, the senior curator of architecture and design at New York City’s MoMA, during a walkthrough of the exhibit as she and her team prepared it for its opening on September 27. “Having an exhibition about information design shows that we’re continuing our mission to talk about the art in our time, of our time.”

The first piece that visitors will see upon entrance through the museum is Warming Stripes, by climatologist Ed Hawkins, who “wanted to find a way to drill it in people’s brains that global warming is really happening.” The stripes, which over the course of the work go from a deep blue to a bright red, represent the average temperature of each year. The imagery resembles a gorgeous rug—and also a huge warning sign. 

To Antonelli, Warming Stripes is an ideal distillation of information design, because the field “takes phenomena big and small, public and intimate, complex, scientific, and statistically more superficial, and renders them in a way that is comprehensible by a wide audience.”

The exhibition shows that information design is not limited to weaving huge data sets into legibility. One portion of Full Disclosure focuses entirely on personal data, and includes a correspondence between artists Giorgia Lupi and Stefanie Posavec. In what became their Dear Data project, the two found creative ways to visualize how many times they cursed in a week, for example. The idea is that the practice of information design can help people connect in a more personal or even playful way with the many nuggets of data that have come to symbolize their lives. 

MoMA has been collecting works of information design since 2008, when Antonelli debuted an exhibition called Design and the Elastic Mind, which focused on the ways designers have adapted to revolutionary scientific change. As part of her curation, she encountered “all of these different designers that didn’t really have a home,” who worked with data visualization, she says. “I kind of hugged them up.” All but one of the pieces in this exhibition are part of MoMA’s collection.

Often, the origination of information design as a practice gets traced back to the invention of the bar chart or Dr. John Snow’s 19th-century map of cholera in London. But Antonelli sees it going back way further—it has always been a part of the human experience because “it’s all about explaining things in a narrative and visual way.” That means cave drawings displaying the haul of deer from a hunt fit the bill, too. 

But the use of computers and digital tools has exploded and expanded the practice of information design. And the exhibition reflects that. 

While many people encounter examples of information design on tiny phone screens, and there are ample opportunities to interact with screens in this exhibition, it also includes massive pieces that take up entire walls or, in the case of Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler’s Calculating Empires, one room. 

Newspapers and media companies often have teams focused on information design, and two works from The New York Times are included in the exhibition—one that uses 3-D rendering to explain why Paris’s Notre Dame cathedral was so vulnerable to fire and another that recreates the Greenwood neighborhood destroyed by the Tulsa race massacre. 

Antonelli sees the museum’s first-ever exhibition focused entirely on information design as a “gentle provocation,” or perhaps a “surprise” reminder that everyday works—say, those found in a newspaper—are museum-worthy.

She wants visitors to leave with a better sense of discernment for the barrage of infographics and diagrams they’ll encounter each day. She hopes they’ll use their own critical sensibility to see how the creator’s choice of color, typeface, or other formal decisions might impact how a viewer sees what it’s trying to represent. And she’d like people who see these design examples to have a keener sense of appreciation for when something has been done “elegantly and efficiently.”

“We’re hoping that, as usual, they will look at their life with different eyes,” Antonelli says. “More critical eyes.”

items.title: [ArchDaily] Patina House / 182 DESIGN
items.content_html: Set within a quiet residential context, Patina House is conceived as an exploration of time through material. Rather than foregrounding form, the design allows materials, craft, and use to shape the experience of the home. The architecture settles into a composed stone envelope that weathers with exposure to the elements, while a curtain of hanging plants forms a living patina, softening the volume over time.

items.title: [ArchDaily] VyD Pavilion / ENNE Arquitectura
items.content_html: In Argentina, a quincho is what we call the space where people gather to eat asados. This project is no exception, but it also serves as an excuse to colonize the back of a corner lot that hosts a single-family home. The architectural typology of the pre-existing house, more suited to a mid-block lot, had deepened the neglect of this empty space, turning it into a "non-place." We took advantage of the commission for the quincho to try to reverse this situation.

items.title: [ArchDaily] casa POP / gon architects
items.content_html: Casa POP is based on the premise that there is no such thing as a standard user, and therefore architecture must adapt to unique ways of living. The original home, a 78 m² apartment located in Vicálvaro, was built in the 2000s under the rigid standards of the traditional nuclear family, resulting in a highly compartmentalized layout full of hallways. This distribution was obsolete for its owners, Santiago and Ángel, a couple whose lives revolve around enjoyment, knowledge, and culture.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Panorama House / Studio B Architecture + Interiors
items.content_html: The Panorama House project involved both renovating and expanding an existing residence originally designed by the renowned mid-century architect, James Hunter. The structure's distinguished heritage and the innovative architectural solution garnered it recognition as a Historic Landmark during the rigorous approval process. Designed for homeowners seeking a peaceful retreat, the residence carefully balances privacy amidst cherished landmarks and bustling trails while embracing the natural beauty of its surroundings.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Light Through the Wall: Indian House Interiors Shaped by Brick Jali
items.content_html: A brick façade does more than define the façade of a house. When designed as a porous screen, it becomes an intermediary between inside and outside, shaping the atmosphere and environmental conditions of the spaces behind it. Across contemporary Indian residential architecture, brick jali — a perforated or lattice brick screen — has been reinterpreted with a contemporary sensibility, drawing on vernacular architectural elements.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Résidence Lourmel / MARS Architectes
items.content_html: Built on a former parking ramp, the Lourmel student housing is conceived as an intermediate figure between the existing buildings and the central garden. Rather than creating a continuous volume, it is divided into four slightly offset blocks. Their shifts and rotations respond to constraints of distance, views and privacy, while opening diagonal perspectives, improving daylight and strengthening connections to the landscape. The volumes gradually recede towards the center of the block, creating a more porous relationship with the street. The existing courtyard is also fully re-landscaped.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Office for Future Converts Former School Into Housing for Displaced Families in Ukraine
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

🔧 ✏️

🔧 ✏️

Office for Future is converting a former school in Stavyshche, Ukraine, into housing for 42 families displaced by the war. Developed for the Charity Foundation Housing for IDP, the project, titled "Dvir – The Shared Courtyard," reuses the approximately 1,900-square-meter building to create 42 apartments and 200 square meters of shared indoor spaces. The intervention combines the existing structure with new timber elements, an energy retrofit, and the transformation of the former asphalt courtyard into a permeable green space.

items.title: [ArchDaily] V Penthouse  / Merckx-Holvoet Architects
items.content_html: Upon entering this apartment, one experiences a design centered on complete rest, with no room for the pressures of daily life. The architects sought an interior that envelops without overwhelming, one that reveals itself slowly rather than all at once. The design centers on poetry and refinement, built around a reduced palette of materials and colors. The intent was to find a threshold of subtlety, a kind of sophistication that does not assert itself but unfolds gradually.

items.title: [Kottke.org] Jimbōchō Book Town
items.content_html:
I visited Jimbōchō today, a neighborhood that’s home to more than 100 used bookstores. Many sell only Japanese books, but some of them have books in English or sell magazines, posters, or visual books that are interesting to browse no matter what language you speak. I visited maybe 20-30 of the stores; here are four of my favorites.

Sawaguchi Book Store features larger format books on art, design, photography, fashion, and architecture. The walls of the staircase are covered in wonderful posters; it took me awhile to climb those stairs. On the second floor, I found a Princess Mononoke movie poster for ¥50,000; tempting. Also on that floor, there’s a small seating area where you can enjoy a beverage out of their two vending machines and quietly read a book or look out the window.

Kitazawa Bookstore. A beautiful old bookstore selling mostly English titles. I spent a lot of time in here browsing. I found a nice leather-bound Pride and Prejudice and a copy of Hemingway’s For Whom the Bell Tolls from the 40s. They had these little notes scattered amongst the shelves gently reminding patrons of the store’s guidelines: “Here, silence helps words to grow. How eahc book with both hands, as if to embrace it.” Another one: “Don’t rush or force the pages wide. Stories, too, are most beautiful when they open slowly.”

Komiyama Shoten is another bookstore specializing in books about art, arcitecture, design, photography, and fashion. I found a cache of old Raygun magazines from the 90s along with a ton of other design books & magazines — on the third floor, I think. On that same floor, they have a collection of erotica and LGBTQ+ books, including a couple of amazing books by Tom of Finland. Lots of great posters throughout the store as well, including a poster for Kids (1995) signed by Larry Clark.

Ohya Shobu features books, woodblock prints, and maps from the Edo and Meiji periods. Super old stuff. The huge map of Edo (Tokyo) in the window is worth the trip by itself. Because everything was so ancient and presumably delicate, I was a bit timid about picking stuff up to look through it, but I’m gonna go back when I’m feeling bolder.

Tags: books · Japan · travel

items.title: [ArchDaily] Between Burning Forests and Utopian Cities: Designing the Climate Transition
items.content_html: There is no shortage of ways to imagine what the world will look like after a climate catastrophe. Genres of movies and novels have been built around the question of what happens when contemporary safeguards fail, from dystopian fiction and post-apocalyptic literature to disaster films, graphic novels, and video games. Burning forests, submerged cities, abandoned infrastructure, resource scarcity, and mass displacement are a familiar visual and narrative vocabulary. We have become remarkably fluent in imagining the consequences of a world that fails to respond to climate change.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Casa Estelí / COLAR Colectivo de Arquitectura
items.content_html: The project is based on a critical and conscious look at the act of building, understanding architecture not as an isolated object, but as a cultural, environmental, and social process deeply linked to the territory and the community that inhabits it. From this perspective, the intervention proposes the conservation and transformation of built heritage as an essential strategy to extend the life of buildings, recognizing the tangible and intangible value they contain. Reclaiming an existing structure does not imply freezing it in time; rather, it means reinterpreting it, allowing it to incorporate new layers of meaning and use, and ensuring it continues to be an active part of the place's evolution.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Designing Domes in the Digital Age: From Concept to Preliminary Estimate
items.content_html: Despite being among architecture's oldest structural forms, domes continue to offer possibilities for creating large, column-free spaces and working with circular or free-form geometries beyond conventional rectangular building types. Their evolution has been closely tied to changes in materials, construction methods, and design tools. Today, digital platforms are adding another layer to this process, allowing some of the decisions traditionally developed later in a project to be explored much earlier.
